Fieldwork Consultancy for the SGBV Care Pathway Study (Addis Ababa)
description:
Tiko Africa Ethiopia invites qualified consultants or firms to carry out a mixed-methods study on screening, service readiness, quality of care and access barriers along the SGBV care pathway for adolescent girls and young women (AGYW) aged 15–24 in Addis Ababa. The consultant will lead the study from data collection through analysis and reporting. 1. Background Tiko is an African non-profit organisation addressing the “Triple Threat” facing adolescent girls and young women in Sub-Saharan Africa: early pregnancy, HIV and sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV). The Triple Threat package, delivered through Tiko’s technology-enabled, community-driven platform, is Tiko’s standard programme in all of its intervention areas. In Addis Ababa, Tiko supports screening, care and referral for survivors of SGBV, and for young women identified through transactional or survival sex screening under the Dignified Livelihoods Initiative (DILI), which adds livelihood support to the Triple Threat package. This study asks where adolescent girls and young women drop out of the SGBV care pathway, and why. It looks at screening and disclosure, service readiness, quality of care, and barriers to access and referral completion. Findings will help Tiko strengthen the SGBV component of the Triple Threat package. The study uses in-depth interviews, key informant interviews, focus group discussions, a short provider survey, and existing Tiko platform and programme records, existing facility readiness (SARA) records, and a review and synthesis of the published and grey literature. The study protocol and English tools are final, subject to the inception review and any ethics conditions, and the ethics review process is underway. The study instruments are: the AGYW in-depth interview guide (Tool 1) with its journey-mapping card (Tool 1a); the provider key informant interview guide (Tool 2); the referral-partner key informant interview guide (Tool 3); the community focus group guide (Tool 4); the provider survey, built in KoboToolbox (Tool 5); the service readiness (SARA) extraction template (Tool 6); and the routine programme data extraction template (Tool 7). Tiko recruits and screens participants for eligibility through its own safe channels. The consultant schedules and conducts the interviews. Sample sizes are targets; any change must be discussed with and approved by Tiko. Tiko's recruitment list assigns each participant's entry route and pathway stage using the rules in protocol Section 7.4.1, including girls identified through both routes and the stage that takes priority when more than one applies. For the transactional or survival sex route, the list also records duration of engagement. Pathway stages. The five stages in the study are: (1) recently screened or identified; (2) accessed one or more services; (3) referred and completed the referral; (4) referred but did not attend; and (5) started services then discontinued. Recruitment aims for about equal numbers per stage within each interview group Tiko will tell the consultant if a stage cannot be filled, and shortfalls are reported, not absorbed into other stages. Sampling and allocation. Tiko will confirm in writing, before fieldwork, the allocation of the 20 provider interviews by cadre (providers, mobilizers, case managers, counsellors), and of the community, caregiver and peer groups. The provider survey includes providers, mobilizers and case managers and covers screening practice, training and protocol awareness, service availability and referral practice. The qualitative samples are not designed for statistical comparison between age groups or pathway stages; differences are described and interpreted qualitatively. 2. Purpose of the consultancy The consultant will carry out ethical, high-quality data collection; transcribe and translate the data; analyze the quantitative and qualitative findings; and write the study report. The consultant works under the direction of the Tiko research team and delivers findings that Tiko can use to improve SGBV screening, service delivery and referral. 3. Scope of work 3.1 Data collection targets -Method - In-depth interviews (IDIs), SGBV screening or disclosure route; Target - 30 (15 aged 15–17; 15 aged 18–24); Participants - AGYW at different pathway stages -Method - IDIs, transactional or survival sex screening route; Target - 20; Participants - AGYW across the five pathway stages -Method - Key informant interviews (KIIs); Target - 32 (20 providers, mobilizers, case managers and counsellors; 12 referral partners); Participants - Service staff and partner organisations -Method - Focus group discussions (FGDs); Target - 6–8 groups of 6–8 people (4–6 community and caregiver groups; 2 peer groups of young women aged 18–24 not enrolled in Tiko services); Participants - Community members, caregivers, peers -Method - Structured provider survey; Target - About 30; Participants - Providers, mobilizers, case managers and counsellors -Method - Secondary data: routine Tiko platform records; Target - All records for study service points in the reference period; Participants - Screening, service and referral data, extracted with Tool 7 -Method - Secondary data: service readiness (SARA) records; Target - All study service points; Participants - Existing facility readiness assessments, extracted with Tool 6 -Method - Literature review and synthesis; Target - Published and grey literature from Ethiopia and comparable urban settings; Participants - Updates the protocol’s review; used to interpret findings 3.2 Activities -Inception. Review the protocol and tools, and agree upon a work plan, field schedule and quality-control plan with Tiko.The inception report also includes: (a) a protocol and tools review that assesses feasibility and recommends any changes, which the Tiko research team reviews and validates before the tools are finalised; (b) a sampling and recruitment strategy explaining how the consultant will work with Tiko's recruitment lists and safe channels to select participants and fill each pathway stage; and (c) a literature review and synthesis that updates the protocol's review with relevant evidence, especially from Ethiopia and other urban settings (maximum 5 pages). Literature findings are reported separately from the study's primary findings and used to interpret the results. -Tools in Amharic. Translate the tools and information sheets from English into Amharic and back-translate them. Resolve differences with the research team with a small number of participants outside the sample, recruited by Tiko under the approved protocol. Tiko submits any substantive change made after translation or piloting to the REC as an amendment, and only REC-approved versions are used in fieldwork. -Field team. Recruit and train female interviewers and facilitators with experience in sensitive research. Training lasts at least five [5] days and covers the protocol, consent and assent, trauma-informed interviewing, safeguarding, referral to psychosocial support and data security. Training also covers the study's interviewing rules (never asking a girl to describe the violence or to confirm her screening result, and non-labelling language for transactional or survival sex), recording service-point codes, and the reporting duty when a girl under 18 discloses abuse. -Data collection. Conduct all interviews, discussions and the survey in private, safe settings, in Amharic. Record audio only with consent. Record the service-point code in the provider survey (Tool 5, A8) and against each service an AGYW describes (Tool 1, Section E), so findings can be linked to the SARA data. -Transcription and translation. Transcribe audio verbatim in Amharic and translate into English. A named reviewer checks at least [10%] of transcripts against the audio. Transcription and translation run progressively during fieldwork, not only at the end, with a fuller check of each interviewer’s first transcripts so quality problems are found early. -Supervision and quality control. Supervise fieldwork daily, review interview notes weekly, and hold debriefs after each fieldwork cycle. -Data handover. Deliver to Tiko: Amharic and English transcripts; audio files; raw and cleaned survey datasets with a codebook; the qualitative codebook and coded project file; completed journey-mapping cards; the consent log, kept separately from the study data; a log of safeguarding incidents and referrals; a protocol-deviation log; and the fieldwork log. All files except the consent log are de-identified. -Analysis. Agree an analysis plan with Tiko. Analyse the qualitative data thematically, using a coding framework and software such as ATLAS.ti. Analyse the survey data descriptively. Triangulate with the service-readiness (SARA) and routine programme data that Tiko provides, and compare findings across pathway stages, entry routes (SGBV screening or disclosure, and transactional or survival sex screening) and age bands. Develop a care-pathway analysis matrix showing, for each pathway stage, where participants enter, where they progress, where and why they discontinue or face barriers, and what supports referral completion and continued care. Assess quality of care against the WHO first-line survivor-centred response (LIVES) and the WHO/UNAIDS Global Standards for quality health care services for adolescents. From the routine data, produce a descriptive screening-to-completion cascade for each entry route, reporting a stage only where its denominator is recorded. Triangulate across AGYW, provider and referral partner interviews, the provider survey and the existing records, and highlight where these perspectives differ. With about 30 survey respondents, survey results are descriptive only and are not presented as representative of all providers in Addis Ababa. The consultant analyses the existing SARA and facility-readiness records and does not collect new facility data unless Tiko agrees in advance. -Validation. Present emerging findings to the Tiko research team and invited stakeholders in one validation meeting, and revise them using the feedback. -Reporting. Submit a draft and a final report (maximum [20] pages plus annexes) with an executive summary, methods, findings by objective, programme and policy recommendations, and a short brief of 3–5 pages for non-technical readers. The discussion interprets the findings against existing evidence and relevant standards (WHO LIVES, the WHO/UNAIDS adolescent quality standards and Ethiopian national SGBV guidelines), noting where findings from Addis Ababa agree with or differ from other settings. Literature findings are kept distinct from the study’s primary findings. Authorship or acknowledgement in any publication follows actual contribution and Tiko’s publication and authorship policy. 3.3 Tiko's responsibilities • Ethics approval and any amendments, with written confirmation before fieldwork starts. • Recruitment and eligibility screening, with recruitment lists showing each participant’s study code, entry route, pathway stage, age band and, for the transactional or survival sex route, duration of engagement. • The study list of service-point codes, and completed SARA and routine-data extraction templates (Tools 6 and 7) for the study service points. • A named psychosocial support focal person on call during fieldwork, and the referral directory. • A data-sharing agreement and the secure storage location for study data. • Tablets and a KoboToolbox account for the provider survey [confirm: Tiko or the consultant]. • Participant reimbursement and interview venues [confirm: paid directly by Tiko, or included in the consultant’s budget]. 4. Ethics, safeguarding and data protection Tiko Africa Ethiopia manages and coordinates the ethics review and Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval process for this study. Applicants and consultants do not need to budget or plan for IRB approval in their proposals. The consultant must follow the final approved protocol, any ethics conditions that Tiko passes on, and the requirements below. Fieldwork starts only when Tiko confirms in writing that approval is in place. Obtain written informed consent from adults and assent from girls aged 15–17.The protocol asks the REC to waive parental permission for girls aged 15–17; if the REC does not grant the waiver, Tiko will issue the revised guardian procedure before fieldwork. Where a girl aged 15–17 has no parent or guardian available (for example, she lives independently, is separated from her family or is street-connected), follow the REC-approved alternative, such as consent from a trusted adult she nominates or an independent advocate appointed by Tiko, so that these girls are not excluded. Use witnessed or thumbprint consent for participants who cannot read, as approved by the REC Do not contact or approach potential participants outside Tiko’s approved recruitment arrangements. Follow the approved protocol when a participant discloses abuse, immediate danger or another safeguarding concern. Make referrals through the approved referral procedure, taking account of the participant’s safety and consent. In focus groups, inform participants during the consent and assent process when deciding to participate that confidentiality is requested from all participants but cannot be guaranteed once information is shared in the group. Interview in private, with a trained female interviewer, and never at a place or time that puts the participant at risk. Do not give incentives beyond the reimbursement approved by the REC. Provide refreshments to all participants. Give AGYW interview and focus group participants the reimbursement for transport and time set out in the approved protocol and consent materials; providers and referral partners interviewed during working hours receive refreshments only. Stop or postpone an interview if the participant is in distress or danger, and link her to Tiko's psychosocial focal person the same day. Report any disclosure of immediate risk, and any safeguarding concern, to the Tiko study coordinator within 24 hours, following the referral and reporting procedure in the protocol. Use participant codes only. Keep names, contacts and recordings on encrypted devices, upload them to the designated Tiko secure storage location, and delete all local copies only after Tiko confirms successful receipt and handover. Delete local audio copies once Tiko confirms the upload and the transcript check is complete. Handle personal data in line with Ethiopian personal data protection law and the data-sharing agreement. Staff and subcontractors sign a confidentiality and code-of-conduct agreement, including Tiko's safeguarding and PSEA policies, before fieldwork. Provide supervisors and interviewers with debriefing and psychosocial support during fieldwork. 5. Deliverables and timeline The schedule below assumes the ethics review is complete before week 1. It will shift if that is delayed: -Deliverable - Contract signing and inception report: work plan, field schedule, analysis plan, quality-control plan; Due - Week 2 -Deliverable - Amharic tools (translated, back-translated, piloted) and training report; Due - Week 5 -Deliverable - Fieldwork progress reports; due - Every 2 weeks during fieldwork -Deliverable - Completion of data collection, submit clean data (transcripts, datasets) and fieldwork log; Due - Week 13 -Deliverable - Draft report with analysis outputs (coded transcripts, survey tables); Due - Week 17 -Deliverable - Validation meeting, final analysis and submission of final report, brief and cleaned dataset; Due - Week 20 Tiko pays within [30] days of accepting each deliverable and gives written comments on each draft within [10] working days. The fieldwork report covers response rates by group, deviations from the protocol, safeguarding incidents, challenges and lessons. The study runs about 20 weeks in total. Each payment depends on Tiko’s written acceptance of the related deliverable. 6. Qualifications and team A lead consultant and a field team. A firm may propose one lead, named supervisors and a named analyst. Team lead. Master’s degree in public health, social science, gender studies or a related field, at least [10] years of social and public health research, including at least [7] years leading qualitative and mixed-methods research on SGBV or adolescent health in Ethiopia, including analysis and report writing. Demonstrated experience leading research with adolescents on sensitive topics, including SGBV or other safeguarding-related research, is required. Field supervisors (2–3). Master’s degree in public health, social science or a related field, and at least [5] years of qualitative fieldwork, including at least [2] years supervising field teams, preferably on gender-based violence or with adolescents. Interviewers and facilitators. Women fluent in Amharic, with at least a bachelor’s degree in social science, public health, nursing or a related field, at least [2] years of qualitative interviewing experience, and training in trauma-informed practice. Experience with adolescents is an advantage. Transcription and translation staff. Native Amharic speakers with strong written English and a record of accurate verbatim transcription. Qualitative data analyst: Master’s degree in a relevant field and at least [5] years in qualitative analysis and in literature review and synthesis, secondary data analysis and triangulation, with proven use of qualitative analysis such as ATLAS.ti or NVivo. The proposal must name who is responsible for qualitative coding and thematic analysis, quantitative data cleaning and descriptive analysis, integration of findings, and report writing. Qualitative analysis experience is assessed separately from skill with statistical software. Quantitative analyst. Degree in a relevant field and at least [5] years analysing survey and secondary programme data with Stata, SPSS or R, including data cleaning, descriptive analysis and triangulation of data from several sources. Either analyst role may be held by the team lead if they meet the requirements. The team lead must show recent ethics-approved research, a working knowledge of Addis Ababa, and a clear safeguarding record. Conflicts of interest, such as current work for Tiko or its partners at study sites, must be declared. 7. Ownership and confidentiality All data, tools, recordings and reports belong to Tiko. The consultant may not share, publish or reuse them without written permission, and the duty of confidentiality continues after the contract ends.

How to Apply: ### **How to apply** Submit the following by December 4th, 2026 to bidding@tiko.org, with the subject line "SGBV Fieldwork Consultancy": 1. A technical proposal (maximum \[8\] pages): understanding of the task, method, approach to the literature review and synthesis, analysis and reporting approach, ethics and safeguarding plan, work plan, and quality-control approach. 2. CVs of the proposed team, with two referees. 3. Examples of two similar assignments, including one on sensitive topics and one report you wrote, and evidence of ethics approval for them. 4. A financial proposal in Ethiopian birr with a line-by-line budget. The ceiling is \[6500 Euro\] including taxes. Participant reimbursement and venue costs are \[included / excluded\] (see Section 3.3). The budget must be itemised: personnel, training, fieldwork, transport, transcription, translation, data management, analysis and reporting. 5. Registration documents and a valid tax clearance, for firms. Evaluation criterion: -Understanding of the task and quality of method, including the analysis and reporting approach - 25% -Ethics, safeguarding and trauma-informed approach - 25% -Team qualifications and relevant experience - 30% -Financial proposal - 20% Only proposals that score at least 70% of the technical points (56 of the 80 points for the first three criteria) have their financial proposals scored. Shortlisted applicants may be interviewed.

title: National Facilitator for Sustainability and Transition Strategy Development
description:
About Asian Disaster Preparedness Center ADPC is a non-profit, autonomous regional organization, international in status, established for scientific, educational, developmental, and humanitarian purposes, with a vision of safer communities and sustainable development through disaster risk reduction. Established in 1986 as an outreach center of the Asian Institute of Technology (AIT), ADPC has evolved into an organization dedicated to building disaster and climate resilience across Asia and the Pacific. ADPC employs a wide range of professional expertise typically required for Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) and Climate Resilience (CR). ADPC develops and implements cross-sectoral projects/programs across the 15 Priority Areas of Action of its Strategic Action Plan 2026–2030: Risk Knowledge and Geoinformatics, Policy and Institutional System, Effective Localization for Resilience, Climate Services, Resilient Planning and Implementation, Preparedness and Anticipatory Action, Nature based Solutions, Financing for Resilience, Resilient Recovery, Food and Water Security, Disaster Risk Finance Insurance, Health Risk Management, Urban & Infrastructure Resilience, Private Sector Engagement, and ADPC Knowledge Academy. These Priority Areas of Action are complemented and underpinned by three cross-cutting enablers: gender equality and social inclusion, disaster and climate innovations, and regional and transboundary cooperation. Through its work, ADPC supports the implementation of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030, the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), the New Urban Agenda, the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, the agenda defined at the World Humanitarian Summit in 2016, and other relevant international frameworks. For details, please refer to the ADPC website at http://www.adpc.net/ . Department Introduction: The Preparedness and Climate Action (PCA) Department of ADPC focuses on enhancing the preparedness, climate action, and adaptation capacities of governments, response organizations, volunteers, non-governmental organizations, the private sector, communities, and other traditional and non-traditional actors within the Disaster Risk Management and Climate Resilience Ecosystem. It emphasizes the importance of locally-led adaptation strategies as a critical component of effective climate action while striving to strengthen the capacity of institutions and at-risk communities to achieve faster, more efficient, and climate-resilient disaster recovery. The department collaborates with these actors to ensure that regional, national, sub-national, and local disaster preparedness, response, recovery, and climate action frameworks and implementation plans are developed and implemented well before disaster strikes, prioritizing climate resilience and integrating strategies to reduce risks and build resilience against future climate-related hazards. Statement of Intent The Preparedness and Climate Action (PCA) Department of the Asian Disaster Preparedness Center (ADPC), in partnership with the Ethiopian Disaster Risk Management Commission (EDRMC), is implementing the E nhancing M ulti-Hazard P reparedness for O ptimizing W arning and Early Response (EMPOWER) Program in Ethiopia, with technical and financial support from the Gates Foundation. The EMPOWER Program aims to strengthen the organizational, institutional and leadership capacities of Ethiopia's disaster risk management institutions at national and subnational levels. It is anchored in the Multi-Hazard, Impact-Based Early Warning and Early Action System (MH-IB-EW-EAS) Roadmap, developed by EDRMC and endorsed by the Government of Ethiopia. Building on previous institutional capacity-building initiatives, EMPOWER seeks to strengthen institutional systems, human resources, technical capacities and coordination mechanisms that can be sustained beyond the program period. As part of these efforts, a Sustainability and Transition Strategy will be developed through an EDRMC-led, consultative and evidence-informed process, with technical support and inputs from ADPC. The process will review institutional capacities, systems and functions developed through successive capacity-building investments, including EMPOWER, to identify what has been sustained, remaining gaps and lessons learned. It will examine priority functions and capacities required to support EDRMC's evolving mandate, appropriate institutional arrangements, resource requirements and feasible sustainability and transition pathways. The findings will also inform EDRMC's longer-term institutional development priorities and potential future programming, with stronger government ownership and sustainability considerations embedded from the outset. In this context, ADPC seeks to engage an experienced national facilitator to support the consultative process and development of the EMPOWER Sustainability and Transition Strategy during the period December 2026 to March 2027. Scope of Work The consultant will work closely with EDRMC leadership, relevant directorates and technical units, with overall coordination and technical support from the ADPC team, to facilitate an EDRMC-led process for developing the Sustainability and Transition Strategy. The consultant's role is to facilitate an objective, structured and participatory process, rather than to independently determine EDRMC's sustainability arrangements. The process will be guided by the principles of EDRMC leadership and ownership; function before financing; institutionalization rather than parallel arrangements; realism and feasibility; progressive transition; and future-oriented programming. 1. Conduct desk review and prepare the consultation framework Review the National Disaster Risk Management Policy (2024), the MH-IB-EW-EAS Roadmap, the EMPOWER program documents and progress reports, and relevant EDRMC policies, institutional strategies, organizational arrangements and capacity-development initiatives, including previous ADPC-supported programs, EMPOWER and other relevant partner-supported investments. Assess the institutional capacity-development journey, identifying key achievements, capacities and systems sustained over time, remaining gaps and lessons learned. Prepare a concise working paper outlining initial findings, institutional sustainability issues and strategic questions for consultation. Develop the consultation methodology, guiding questions and workplan in coordination with EDRMC and ADPC, and establish a common understanding with EDRMC leadership on the purpose, scope and expected results of the exercise. 2. Facilitate Institutional Consultations, Sustainability Assessment and Strategic Planning Facilitate consultations with EDRMC leadership, directorates and technical units to identify priority institutional functions, capacities and systems required to fulfil EDRMC's evolving mandate under the National DRM Policy (2024), including functional linkages with sector ministries and sub-national DRM structures. Assess institutional ownership, existing capacities, human resources and surge-capacity arrangements, operational and ICT systems and their recurrent costs (e.g., software licences, hardware, situation room and data-server infrastructure), resource requirements, partnerships and sustainability challenges, taking into account previous investments in institutional capacity building. Examine feasible institutionalization and sustainability arrangements, including integration into government structures, capacity transfer, recurrent financing and continued technical or partner support. Develop a sustainability and institutionalization mapping, presenting options for discussion rather than predetermined commitments, that captures priority functions, institutional responsibilities, resource requirements, sustainability options and lessons learned from previous capacity-building investments. Facilitate strategic consultations with EDRMC, ADPC and, as appropriate, the Gates Foundation to review assessment findings and identify feasible sustainability and transition pathways. Support discussions on institutional priorities, ownership, financing options, partnerships and progressive transition of technical support, with a focus on strengthening EDRMC's long-term institutional capacity for disaster risk reduction, resilience building and self-reliance, including its ability to coordinate, operate, maintain and improve the MH-IB-EW-EAS using its own structures, people, procedures and resources after EMPOWER ends. Identify institutional or policy matters requiring higher-level government decisions and propose appropriate engagement approaches to secure necessary institutional commitments and resources. Document agreed directions, outstanding issues and strategic considerations for potential future capacity-development programming. 3. Develop and finalize the Sustainability and Transition Strategy Prepare a draft EDRMC-led Sustainability and Transition Strategy and Action Plan, drawing on consultation findings, institutional priorities and agreed strategic directions. Develop a practical, phased action plan identifying priority actions, institutional responsibilities, indicative timelines, resource considerations and sustainability indicators, including actions that can begin during the remaining EMPOWER implementation period. Facilitate review of the draft and a validation discussion with EDRMC, ADPC and the Gates Foundation, as appropriate, to confirm the proposed sustainability pathways, institutional responsibilities and priority actions. Incorporate feedback and submit the final Strategy and Action Plan by 10 March 2027 . Expected Deliverables This is an output-based consultancy. Payment will be made upon acceptance of each deliverable by ADPC, in consultation with EDRMC, as follows: Deliverable 1 – [20]%; Deliverable 2 – [40]%; Deliverable 3 – [40]%. The consultant is expected to deliver the following: Inception Report and Consultation Framework: Outlining the methodology, workplan, initial mapping of programs’ supported functions, the working paper on emerging sustainability issues and strategic questions for consultation, preliminary review of EDRMC's institutional capacity-development journey, lessons from previous capacity-building investments, and proposed consultation approach. Institutional Sustainability Assessment and Consultation Report: Consolidating findings from institutional and strategic consultations, including priority functions, existing capacities, institutional responsibilities, sustainability challenges, resource and financing requirements, and feasible institutionalization and transition options. The report will include the sustainability and institutionalization matrix and document key stakeholder discussions, agreed directions, outstanding issues and priority actions. Sustainability and Transition Strategy and Action Plan: Developed in consultation with EDRMC and reflecting assessment findings and agreed sustainability priorities. The strategy will outline institutional responsibilities, phased actions, resource requirements, milestones, and indicators to strengthen long-term institutional capacity, disaster risk reduction, resilience building and self-reliance. It will include a priority action plan for the remaining EMPOWER implementation period and strategic considerations for potential future programming in Ethiopia. The final version will incorporate feedback from EDRMC, ADPC and the Gates Foundation, as appropriate. Deliverable 1: Inception Report & Consultation Framework Timeline: Dec 2026 Deliverable 2: Institutional Sustainability Assessment and Consultation Report Timeline: Jan-Feb 2027 Deliverable 3: Sustainability Strategy Timeline: Feb - Mar 2027 Working Principles: In performing the duties and responsibilities above, the consultant will be supervised by the ADPC Program Manager based in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, and work in close coordination with a designated EDRMC focal point, who will facilitate access to relevant directorates, personnel and information. ADPC will provide relevant documentations and evidence and will support the organization of consultation and validation meetings. All deliverables will be reviewed by EDRMC and ADPC prior to acceptance. Required Qualifications and Experience The consultant should demonstrate the following: Postgraduate degree in Disaster Risk Management, Public Policy, Public Administration, Institutional Development, Development Studies, or a related field. At least 7 years of relevant professional experience in institutional capacity development, organizational strengthening, strategic planning, or sustainability and transition planning, preferably within government or public-sector institutions. Proven experience in facilitating institutional assessments, strategic consultations, and multi-stakeholder planning processes, particularly with government leadership and technical departments. Demonstrated experience in developing institutional sustainability strategies, transition plans, capacity development frameworks, or related strategic and operational plans, including practical implementation arrangements. Good understanding of disaster risk management, multi-hazard early warning systems, and institutional arrangements for disaster preparedness and response. Experience assessing institutional functions, human resource capacities, operational systems, financing requirements, and options for sustaining externally supported investments. Familiarity with government institutional structures, planning and budgeting processes, and coordination mechanisms in Ethiopia; prior experience with EDRMC or the national DRM system is an advantage. Strong analytical, stakeholder engagement, facilitation, and report-writing skills, with the ability to translate consultation findings into actionable recommendations, responsibilities, milestones, and resource considerations. Experience working with government institutions, development partners, and international organizations is highly desirable. Excellent proficiency in English and Amharic is required. description:
Cordaid is an international organisation for development and humanitarian assistance, working especially in fragile and conflict-affected regions. Guided by Christian values of human dignity, justice and compassion, we work towards a world without poverty and with equitable opportunities for all. More than 1.9 billion people live in fragile contexts where access to essential services and opportunities is limited. Together with our partners, we support locally led programmes in longer term development that strengthen healthcare, education, agrifood and justice systems. When crises occur, we work alongside local organisations to provide humanitarian assistance. Cordaid has regional offices in Europe, West-Africa, Horn, East, Central and South Africa and in the Middle East and Asia. Cordaid operates through a domain-based model. Our regional and country teams work with local partners so they can lead humanitarian response. Cordaid provides the local actors with capacity, technical advice and helps them meet humanitarian standards, engage with donors and fulfil their commitments. Cordaid is looking for a Regional Humanitarian Manager - Horn, Eastern, Central and Southern Africa (HECSA) (Fulltime, home-based in the HECSA region) As our Regional Humanitarian Manager for HECSA, you provide strategic leadership for humanitarian action, emergency preparedness, and crisis response across the region. Working at the interface between the HECSA Regional Core and the global Humanitarian Assistance Platform, you ensure that humanitarian responses are principled, locally led, and effectively integrated into regional strategies and Country Engagement Models (triple nexus approach). You serve as the organization's primary regional humanitarian focal point, representing HECSA in regional humanitarian coordination, policy, and advocacy spaces, and building strategic relationships with key stakeholders, first and above our networks of Caritas and ACT Alliance and also including UN agencies, donors, INGOs, regional bodies, and local humanitarian actors. Rather than managing direct programme implementation, you enable local partners to lead by strengthening preparedness, technical quality, and organisational readiness. You report directly to the HECSA Regional Director and to the global humanitarian manager. What you do Humanitarian Leadership & Strategy : Provide strategic leadership and advice on humanitarian action across the HECSA region, supporting Regional Directors and Country Engagement Models in rapid crisis decision-making Emergency Preparedness & Response : Strengthen regional preparedness and crisis readiness by coordinating regional contingency planning and supporting emergency response activations, Humanitarian Partnerships & Localisation : Foster equitable partnerships with national and local humanitarian partners across HECSA, with a partner led approach. Triple Nexus & Sectoral Integration : Spearhead the humanitarian-development-peace nexus approach across the region, linking emergency response and recovery to longer-term resilience, climate adaptation, and systems strengthening. Technical quality and accountability : Work with Cordaid’s global humanitarian team to uphold humanitarian principles, apply the Core Humanitarian Standard and the Sphere Standards, integrate protection across programmes, and ensure that crisis-affected people can give feedback and receive a response. Resource Mobilization & Positioning : Support engagement with major institutional humanitarian donors (ECHO, BHA, Dutch Relief Alliance, UN agencies) and work closely with the Business Development Manager to build a healthy regional humanitarian funding pipeline. Networking, Representation & Advocacy : Represent the Regional Core in regional humanitarian coordination clusters, UN/OCHA meetings, ACT Alliance and Caritas (country) fora, INGO platforms, and donor forums to advance strategic priorities and advocate for locally led responses. Risk Management, Safeguarding & Integrity : Implement Cordaid’s Integrity Compliance Framework, manage operational and contextual risks in fragile environments, and champion high standards of duty of care and safety. Who you are You hold a Master’s degree in Humanitarian Assistance, International Development, Disaster Management, International Relations, or a related field. Minimum of 10 years of progressively responsible experience in humanitarian leadership, emergency response, and crisis management in complex, fragile, and conflict-affected environments. Evidence of leading emergency responses in fragile settings, working with local partners that lead delivery, and representing an organisation with donors and humanitarian coordination bodies. Deep knowledge of the humanitarian sector and complex crisis dynamics across Horn, Eastern, Central or Southern Africa (HECSA). Sound practical expertise in Core Humanitarian Standards (CHS), SPHERE guidelines, cash transfer modalities, protection mainstreaming, and the triple nexus approach. Proven track record in working through national/local partners, driving localisation, and supporting partner capacity sharing in emergency settings. Demonstrated experience engaging with institutional humanitarian donors (ECHO, BHA, DRA, UN/CBHF) and multi-stakeholder humanitarian networks. Strong strategic thinking, decision-making, analytical, and financial management skills. Exceptional oral and written communication skills in English. Proficiency in French, Portuguese, Arabic, or relevant regional languages is a distinct advantage. Willingness to be home-based in the HECSA region with flexibility to travel up to 50% of the time within the region. You recognize yourself in Cordaid’s mission and values. What we offer A high-profile senior leadership position within an international, professional organization with a focus on social impact. A varied, highly impactful, and autonomous role where strategic initiative and vision are essential. A global organization with a strong commitment to social entrepreneurship and locally led impact. Good international working conditions and excellent secondary benefits. An initial contract for 1 year with the intention of extending, home-based within the HECSA region.

Your application must be received by **30 November 2026** at the latest. Cordaid is fully committed to a safe working environment and the highest integrity standards. To read more on our commitment to Integrity, click here: [https://www.cordaid.org/en/who-we-are/integrity-and-code-of-conduct/](https://www.cordaid.org/en/who-we-are/integrity-and-code-of-conduct/). An integrity screening will be part of this application procedure. Cordaid signed up to the IASC Misconduct Disclosure Scheme. An assessment and / or a presentation of a “case study” can be part of the selection procedure. For more information about Cordaid, please visit our website: [www.cordaid.org](http://www.cordaid.org/) *Acquisition regarding this vacancy is not appreciated.*

title: Terms of References (ToR) for a Consultancy to Conduct a Feasibility Study for the proposed project: A Voice for Inclusion.
description:
Terms of References (ToR) for a Consultancy to Conduct a Feasibility Study for the proposed project: A Voice for Inclusion – Equal Education and a Strong Civil Society for Children with Disabilities in Ethiopia, The Gambia and Zambia. Assignment period: December 2026 – January 2027 Location:Ethiopia, The Gambia and Zambia Commissioned by:ChildFund Main Partners: ChildFund Deutschland, ChildFund Ethiopia, ChildFund The Gambia, ChildFund Zambia, Tesfa Birhan, Saama Kairo Federation, Chibombo/Mumbwa Child Development Agency, Kafue Child Development Agency Donor: Project to be submitted to BMZ Background and Context Context of the assignment Despite the ratification of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD) by Ethiopia (in 2010), The Gambia (in 2015) and Zambia (in 2010), many children with disabilities continue to face significant barriers to accessing and successfully completing primary education. Children with severe or multiple disabilities, intellectual or learning disabilities, sensory impairments, and disabilities that remain unidentified are often among the most excluded. Exclusion is further compounded by factors such as gender, age, poverty and geographical remoteness. In addition, the absence of systematic processes for identifying children with disabilities frequently limits their access to appropriate support services, accommodations and referral mechanisms. Preliminary problem analyses conducted in all three countries suggest a number of common barriers and root causes. At family and community level, these include poverty and disability-related costs, transport and distance barriers, limited awareness of available support services, stigma and discrimination, weak parent support structures, safety concerns, and low expectations regarding the educational potential of children with disabilities. At school level, challenges include inadequate teacher preparation for inclusive education, insufficient follow-up coaching and mentoring, limited availability of assistive devices and adapted learning materials, inaccessible infrastructure, overcrowded classrooms, and constrained institutional and financial resources. Across all three countries, gaps are also evident between national policy commitments and their implementation at district, community and school levels. Common issues include weak coordination between sectors and administrative levels, insufficient funding, limited use of disability-disaggregated data, weak referral systems, and limited opportunities for meaningful participation of children with disabilities and their caregivers in planning and decision-making processes. In Zambia, UNCRPD commitments are domesticated through the Persons with Disabilities Act No. 6 of 2012, which provides for the right to inclusive education and established the Zambia Agency for Persons with Disabilities (ZAPD), alongside the Education Act of 2011 and the Children’s Code Act of 2022. The free education policy introduced in 2022 removed school fees, yet children with disabilities in rural and peri-urban districts such as Kafue, Mumbwa and Chibombo continue to face barriers that fee removal alone does not address, including distance to school, limited district-level assessment and specialised services, few teachers trained in inclusive or special education, and stigma. In The Gambia, commitments under the UNCRPD are supported by the Disability Act (2021), the Children’s Act, and the Ministry of Basic and Secondary Education’s Inclusive Education Policy Framework. Despite these policy commitments, children with disabilities continue to face significant barriers to accessing quality education, including late identification of disabilities, limited availability of specialised assessment and support services, inadequate assistive and learning resources, social stigma, and insufficient capacity within mainstream schools to respond to diverse learning needs. These challenges are often more pronounced in rural and underserved communities. In Ethiopia, commitments to inclusive education are operationalised through the Constitution (Article 41), the education policy framework, and the current Special Needs/Inclusive Education Strategy (2022/23-2029/30), which aims to ensure equitable access to quality education for children, youth and adults with special educational needs and disabilities. Despite this strong policy commitment, significant barriers continue to hinder implementation at federal, regional, woreda and school levels, including weak disability data systems, limited early identification and referral mechanisms, shortages of trained inclusive education professionals, inadequate assistive devices and adapted learning materials, inaccessible infrastructure, and persistent stigma. These challenges are often compounded by poverty, displacement, geographical isolation and gender-related disadvantages, particularly in rural, pastoralist, conflict-affected and underserved communities. While the analyses point to significant similarities in the patterns of exclusion across Ethiopia, The Gambia and Zambia, they are also highlighting important contextual differences. This creates opportunities for structured cross-country learning, knowledge exchange and the adaptation of effective approaches across different contexts. The planned project aims to address these challenges with an integrated micro-meso-macro approach: communities and families are sensitized and empowered; schools are developed into inclusive learning environments, mainly through training and development plans; and civil society organisations are strengthened to carry out advocacy work for inclusive education. The multi-country nature of the program offers an opportunity to generate evidence, promote cross-learning and identify scalable approaches that can strengthen inclusive education systems beyond the targeted locations. Inclusive education is both a rights-based obligation and a strategic investment in human capital, social inclusion and sustainable development. Ensuring that children with disabilities can access and succeed in education contributes to national development priorities, advances SDG 4 commitments, and supports broader efforts to ensure that no child is left behind. Brief about ChildFund International as the organization commissioning the study ChildFund International is a global child- and youth-focused development and humanitarian organization dedicated to advancing the well-being, resilience, and rights of children and young people, particularly those facing vulnerability and exclusion. Working through local partners, communities, governments, and civil society, ChildFund promotes locally led and owned development approaches that strengthen systems, build community capacity, and create sustainable impact for children and their families. Its programmes focus on education, child protection, health, livelihoods, and youth empowerment, with an emphasis on achieving lasting outcomes that enable children and young people to learn, thrive, and contribute meaningfully to their communities. This assignment is commissioned by ChildFund International to inform the design and implementation of a multi-country inclusive education programme in Ethiopia, The Gambia, and Zambia. The International Office (IO) will provide overall strategic direction, technical leadership, and quality assurance; the Africa Regional Office (RO) will provide regional coordination, technical oversight, and facilitate cross-country learning; while the respective Country Offices (COs) will lead country-level coordination, stakeholder engagement, and contextual guidance to ensure the study reflects national priorities and local realities. Brief about the proposed project The proposed multi-country programme seeks to improve equitable access to, participation in, and quality of inclusive primary education for children with disabilities in Ethiopia, The Gambia, and Zambia. The programme is founded on the recognition that educational exclusion results from interconnected barriers at household, community, school, and systems levels, requiring a coordinated and multi-level response. Through a locally grounded and systems-strengthening approach, the programme aims to ensure that children with disabilities, including those who are currently out of school, are identified, enrolled, actively engaged in learning, and able to make measurable progress in foundational literacy and numeracy. Particular attention will be given to children facing multiple and intersecting forms of exclusion, including girls with disabilities, children with high support needs, children living in poverty, and those in remote or underserved areas. To achieve these outcomes, the programme will pursue an integrated micro-meso-macro approach that combines community engagement, inclusive school development, institutional capacity strengthening, and policy engagement through four complementary result areas. Proposed Output 1: Family and Community Environment Children with disabilities will be identified through community-based identification and referral mechanisms. Parents/caregivers will be supported to promote school enrolment and effectively address the learning needs of children with disabilities, including through effective referral systems and linkages to service providers, in line with the programme's systems-strengthening and sustainability objectives. Parents/caregiver self-help groups will be established and/or strengthened to address barriers to education and support sustained participation, retention, and educational success for children with disabilities. Proposed Output 2: Inclusive Schools and Learning Environments Target schools will be supported to strengthen inclusive teaching and learning practices through teacher training, coaching and mentoring and the development of learning materials and methods aligned with the needs of children with disabilities. Existing school structures will be trained and supported to introduce inclusive school development plans, thereby embedding inclusive practices within school systems and leadership structures to support long-term implementation, ownership, and scalability beyond the life of the programme. Model schools will be equipped with accessible infrastructure, demonstrating how accessible learning environments contribute to sustainable institutional change and improved learning outcomes; while other project schools will be supported to identify, prioritise and cost accessibility improvements, with project funding complementing local resources and budgets where available. Proposed Output 3: Civil Society Capacity and Advocacy Through cross-national learning and collaboration, civil society organisations will strengthen their capacity to generate and use evidence on effective and cost-efficient inclusive education practices, engage in evidence-based advocacy, and promote the active participation of persons with disabilities and their representatives in education policy processes. A joint cross-national platform will facilitate the long-term exchange of evidence, implementation experiences, costing data and advocacy tools to support the institutionalisation and financing of inclusive education practices. Proposed Output 4: Policy Implementation and Local Adoption Under Output 4, civil society organisations and OPDs will be supported to translate evidence and lessons learned from project implementation and cross-country exchange into advocacy messages, policy recommendations and budget proposals for inclusive education. Through engagement with policy-makers, planning bodies and coordination mechanisms, opportunities will be created to foster government ownership and to promote the uptake of effective and cost-efficient inclusive education practices within planning, budgeting and resource allocation processes. This will support the use of evidence to inform scalable and sustainable system-level improvements, strengthen the institutionalisation of inclusive education practices within government systems, and contribute to the sustained delivery of inclusive education services beyond the project period. Through these interconnected interventions, the programme aims to contribute to a situation in which children with disabilities in the target communities are able to enrol in school, participate effectively in classroom learning and achieve measurable improvements in foundational literacy and numeracy. In the longer term, the programme seeks to strengthen inclusive education systems and support the sustainable implementation of inclusive education policies and practices across the three participating countries. Purpose and Scope of the Feasibility Study Study Type A feasibility study provides an evidence-based foundation for project design and investment decisions by assessing implementation readiness, opportunities, risks, and key assumptions and offering guidance and possible improvements. The findings will inform programme optimisation and effectiveness, identify pathways for sustainable and scalable impact, and help ensure that resources are directed towards interventions with the greatest potential to improve inclusive education outcomes. Purpose of the Study The purpose of the feasibility study is particularly to assess the feasibility of the proposed project and systematically examine the extent to which the project approach can plausibly achieve the planned changes under the existing conditions. Specifically, the study focuses on these specific topics: 1. Evidence Base and Context Analysis Identify and review relevant international, regional and national evidence related to disability-inclusive primary education, including successful approaches, lessons learned, policy frameworks, implementation models and emerging good practices. Establish baseline information on the current situation of children with disabilities, schools, communities and relevant stakeholders in the target areas in order to inform project design and future monitoring. All proposed baseline data should be disaggregated by region/district, sex, age, grade/educational level and type of disability. Map existing systems, services, structures and coordination mechanisms relevant to disability-inclusive education and determine where the project should strengthen existing systems, fill critical gaps or avoid duplication of existing initiatives. 2. Relevance and Strategic Fit Evaluate the relevance of the proposed project activities, objectives and strategies in relation to the needs of target groups, existing systems and the broader context. Assess the strategic rationale and expected added value of the proposed multi-country approach compared to separate country-level interventions. The study should analyse common challenges, complementary strengths, opportunities for cross-country learning, joint advocacy, knowledge exchange, mutual capacity development and the transfer of effective inclusive education practices, as well as factors that justify the selection of Ethiopia, The Gambia and Zambia as participating countries. Recommend practical and financially realistic strategies for ensuring that the project benefits children with different types of disabilities, including those who are often most excluded, such as children with intellectual disabilities, communication difficulties, multiple disabilities and higher support needs. 3. Validation of the Proposed Intervention Validate the project's Theory of Change, he proposed indicators, baseline and target values and recommend revisions where necessary to ensure realistic and measurable results; also assess the plausibility of the proposed causal pathways and expected outcomes. Assess how the proposed intervention can most effectively contribute to meaningful participation and measurable improvements in foundational literacy and numeracy outcomes for children with disabilities. The study should identify critical success factors, potential barriers and additional measures required to ensure that increased enrolment and attendance translate into improved learning outcomes. Assess the availability and capacity of existing systems for feasible, ethically appropriate, disability-responsive assessment, identification, referral and learning support/educational-support pathways, referral completion, feedback loops, case follow-up and service-capacity constraints. This should include an analysis of whether learning assessments can be adapted to different impairments, the uptake of Universal Design for Learning in the target schools so far, the availability of specialised teaching and learning materials and assistive devices, and the capacity of government services, OPDs and other actors to assess children's needs and facilitate access to appropriate support. Test key assumptions underlying the project design, including assumptions related to identification and referral systems, teacher retention, stakeholder engagement, service availability, maintenance of infrastructure, the added value of cross-country learning and the sustainability of project-supported approaches. Assess the feasibility of local adoption and financing of tested inclusive education practices by schools, local authorities and government structures, including opportunities for incorporation into existing planning, budgeting, supervision and school improvement systems Assess the integration of cross-cutting issues, including gender equality, child safeguarding, conflict sensitivity and environmental sustainability. 4. Capacity and Feasibility Assessment Assess the operational feasibility of the proposed intervention, including availability of resources, institutional arrangements and stakeholder commitment at community, district and national levels. Assess the organisational and technical capacities of the proposed implementing partners and evaluate whether the proposed intervention is realistic and proportionate to their current capacities. The study should identify existing strengths, capacity gaps and the capacity development measures required to enable partners to successfully implement, monitor and sustain the proposed interventions. Identify external factors, contextual influences and implementation risks that may affect the achievement and sustainability of project results. Assess the likelihood that project-supported approaches, services and practices can be sustained, institutionalised and financed by local actors after project completion. 5. Optimisation and Recommendations Assess the extent to which the proposed project design is realistic within the available budget and identify opportunities for simplification, prioritisation and cost-efficiency. Review and, where necessary, refine the proposed intervention strategy, impact matrix, outputs and indicators (including baseline and target values) based on study findings, including the development of recommendations for indicators and targets that have not yet been defined. Provide evidence-based recommendations for improving project design, implementation arrangements, targeting, monitoring, partnership development, capacity strengthening, sustainability and scalability Assessment Criteria The study should present the context of the planned project at all relevant levels (micro, meso, macro) and also include key data relevant to the project regarding the initial situation. Building on this, an analysis should be carried out to determine the extent to which the chosen approach can contribute to resolving the problem for the target groups and other stakeholders. Recommendations for adjustments to the specific project concept – including the draft impact matrix and suggested measures – should be formulated in as concrete a manner as possible. In doing so, consideration must be given to the actors and stakeholders to be involved, proposals for areas to be monitored in terms of outcome and impact measurement, and the opportunities and risks involved. Furthermore, the proposed project should be critically assessed in the light of the OECD DAC criteria of relevance, coherence, effectiveness, efficiency, impact and sustainability: Relevance: Does the planned project approach address a key development issue or a critical development bottleneck in the partner countries? Are the focus, priorities and objectives (approach) of the planned project aligned with the target groups and clearly defined? To what extent do the intervention objectives and design adequately take into account the specific needs of the target groups and structural barriers in the project countries, the partner organisations, and the political programmes? Are the norms and standards of the approach compatible with those of the target groups? Is the project designed with conflict sensitivity in mind (the ‘Do No Harm’ principle)? Coherence: To what extent are the planned activities consistent with human rights principles (inclusion, participation), conventions and relevant standards/guidelines? To what extent are there synergies and links between the planned project and other interventions by the same partners and other actors? What overlaps or common ground exist between the target groups of this project and those of other actors’ projects in the same context? To what extent does the intervention add value and avoid duplication of effort? Effectiveness: Are the causal relationships (including assumptions) plausible? What negative effects might arise? Is the chosen methodological approach appropriate to the context and sufficient to achieve the project’s objective? At what level (multi-level approach) should additional measures be planned to increase effectiveness? How will changes be measured (baseline and endline tools)? Are the indicators in the draft impact matrix suited for this? Efficiency: To what extent can the planned measures be implemented within the planned timeframe and allocated funds? Which staffing investments, operating costs and staffing levels are recommended proportionate to the intended objectives? Impact: How does the project objective (outcome) contribute specifically to the overarching objective (impact)? To what extent does the planned project contribute to structural development, serve as a model and have a broad, cross-national impact beyond progress within each country and beyond the project period? At what levels are standards or structures being changed? Sustainability: How can the sustainability of the results and impacts be ensured and strengthened (structurally, economically, socially, environmentally)? What long-term capacities are being built up within the target group to enable them to continue the implemented measures independently? What positive changes (role behaviour, mechanisms, networks and others) benefit civil society in the long term? What personnel risks for those implementing the measures, as well as institutional and contextual risks, affect sustainability, and how can these be minimised? On the basis of the key findings relating to the purpose of the study and the assessment of the project concept against the DAC criteria, the study should make clear recommendations which specific proposals and improvements should be incorporated into the project concept. Key assessment questions Building on the specific topics described above and the OECD-DAC criteria described, the study should address the following key questions: 1. Purpose and use of the feasibility study How conducive is the context (sector, components, project regions) with regard to the projects’ objective? How feasible is achieving the proposed project outcome and the underlying Theory of Change as well as the proposed indicators? And how coherent is the proposed intervention across sectors, outputs and countries? Which critical assumptions underpin the project's Theory of Change, and to what extent are these assumptions supported by available evidence and stakeholder perspectives? Which factors are most likely to influence whether increased enrolment and attendance translate into improved learning outcomes for children with disabilities? How can the study findings contribute to adaptive management, organisational learning and project refinement across all three countries? 2. Methodology What participatory methods, tools, and resources will be used for data collection and analysis (incl. recommendation of baseline and endline tools)? Which stakeholders will be involved? What are their backgrounds and interests? How can meaningful participation of children with disabilities, caregivers, schools, civil society organisations, OPDs and government stakeholders be ensured? 3. Initial situation and problem analysis, on macro- meso- and micro-levels What current problems of children with disabilities have been identified at micro, meso and macro levels, relevant to the proposed project? Which of the causes of these problems will be prioritised and addressed in the project? What existing root causes, local potential, structures (institutions, networks, umbrella organizations etc.) and social mechanisms can be built on? What gaps have been identified in the system? Which existing identification, referral, assessment and support systems for children with disabilities are functioning effectively and where do significant gaps remain? What specialised teaching and learning materials, assistive devices and support services are currently available, and where are the most significant gaps? To what extent can existing education assessment systems be adapted to different impairment groups, and what constraints currently limit equitable assessment of learning outcomes? What currently prevents children with disabilities from progressing from enrolment to meaningful participation and improvements in foundational literacy and numeracy? Are there any approaches or results from previous development measures? If yes, how can they be extended? Which existing government, community and OPD structures should be strengthened rather than duplicated by the project? What other circumstances, for example conflict dynamics, must be taken into account in the context of the selected countries? 4. Local project partners in the partner countries Which organisations have been selected as local project partners, and why? How will the local project partners’ ownership be improved? Are the partners’ resources and strengths, both individually and at an organisational level, well understood? To what extent does the project planning align with the current capacities of the local partners Tesfa Birhan, Saama Kairo Federation, Chibombo/Mumbwa Child Development Agency, Kafue Child Development Agency? Is selective support from staff of the ChildFund International Country Offices necessary and justified and which project functions can realistically be led by the local partners themselves? What coordination structure between the local partners is recommended? What relevant technical, methodological and advocacy competencies will be further developed within the local partners through the project to strengthen their long-term capacity for implementation, coordination and advocacy? 5. Beneficiaries and other stakeholders (on a micro-, meso- and macro-level) How (with which criteria) will the direct beneficiaries be selected, and by whom? Which groups of children with disabilities are most likely to benefit from the proposed intervention as currently designed, and which groups may require adapted approaches or additional support measures? How is the diversity within the target groups, including disability type, age, gender, socio-economic situation and location, and to what extent must the project take this into account? How can different disability groups can be meaningfully included and the proposed interventions be adapted to address the specific needs of different impairment groups and support requirements? What potential do the beneficiaries have for self-help? Do the beneficiaries and other stakeholders have a common understanding of the problems, prioritising process and objectives of the project? Do the interests of other stakeholders align? Do any conflicts of interest exist? How strong is the various stakeholders’ support for the project, for example, in terms of their own contribution? In what ways might they influence the project? 6. Multi-Country Dimension What is the added value of implementing the proposed project with a multi-country approach compared to stand-alone country projects? What common objective – beyond progress within each country – justifies the multi-country approach? Does this justify the additional complexity and coordination effort of a three-country programme? What is the rationale for the selection of Ethiopia, The Gambia and Zambia? What are the relationships between the three project countries and what are shared and country-specific barriers, opportunities for cross-country learning and potential for joint advocacy and knowledge exchange? Could a project with only two countries achieve similar results more effectively? What existing (cross-national) structures does the project build upon, and what will remain after the project ends? How can sustainability be ensured across all three countries, and into which umbrella organization, active in all three countries, can results of the project be incorporated; and what lasting mechanisms for cooperation, joint learning and advocacy could be established or strengthened? 7. Strategic and Financial Feasibility How realistic is the proposed intervention design under the available budget envelope? Are any adjustments required to the indicators, baseline and target values to ensure they are achievable, measurable and aligned with the proposed intervention design and budget? What are potential simplifications and prioritization options, and which project components are essential to preserve the intended outcomes and Theory of Change? Which elements of the proposed intervention are most likely to be institutionalised and financed by local actors after project completion, and what mechanisms or arrangements are required to sustain both project results and cross-country cooperation beyond external funding? Study Methodology The study will comprise both desk-based research and fieldwork. It will involve a combination of primary data collection and secondary data review. Selected secondary data sources will be made available to the contractor. The following documents will be provided: Initial concept note for the planned project Draft impact matrix Draft theory of change Initial problem analysis conducted by the partners Partner documents relevant to the planned project Selected national strategy documents, background papers, references For the collection of primary data, the contractor is encouraged to propose appropriate methodological approaches (quantitative, qualitative, or mixed methods). The study methodology should, where appropriate and ethically feasible, include the direct participation of the project’s primary target group – children with disabilities. The study should ensure that the voices and perspectives of children with disabilities and their families are reflected in the findings, particularly with regard to their participation in project activities and perceived changes in their living conditions. The contractor is expected to propose appropriate, age-sensitive, and ethically sound data collection methods for engaging with children and youths, in line with relevant safeguarding and ethical standards. In addition, the study should include the following data collection methodologies: Desk and literature review Stakeholder consultations Field visits Key Informant Interviews with partner staff, community leaders, and other relevant stakeholders Focus Group Discussions with intended target groups Household or individual surveys (quantitative data collection) Workshop/validation meeting to review preliminary findings with partners and stakeholders Ethical Consideration It is essential to ensure that the risks of potential harm to participants arising from the data collection process are minimized and clearly outweighed by the potential benefits of the study’s outcomes. The contractor must address critical ethical issues in the design and implementation of the study, ensuring that the rights, safety, and confidentiality of all information providers are fully protected. Key considerations include, but are not limited to: Compliance with legal and regulatory requirements, including permissions for data collection, storage, export, and, where applicable, interviewing or collecting information about children and youth. For Zambia: Research ethics clearance from the Research Ethics Committee, and authorisation from the National Health Research Authority (NHRA) where health-related data (e.g., functional screening) are collected; written authority from the Ministry of Education and the respective DEBS offices to conduct research in schools; and compliance with the Data Protection Act No. 3 of 2021 and the Children’s Code Act of 2022. For The Gambia : IRB approval from the university of the Gambia (UTG), Compliance with national child protection and safeguarding regulations, relevant data protection requirements, approvals from MoBSE and Regional Education Directorates, and adherence to ChildFund safeguarding standards when engaging children with disabilities and their caregivers. For Ethiopa : Determine whether ethics review is required, secure federal/regional/woreda and school permissions, and comply with Personal Data Protection Proclamation No. 1321/2024, including special protections for children, disability/health data, storage and cross-border transfer Measures to ensure the secure storage and management of collected data.
